In particular, we re-examine the circular Couette analogy that underpins both the physical interpretation of the flow and the extraction of flow curves from raw rheometric data. Based on our extensive two- and three-dimensional simulations, we identify limitations of the existing conversion relations and propose improved closure expressions that enable more accurate determination of material's rheological properties. Furthermore, the three-dimensional flow structures and yielding patterns within the vane-in-cup fixtures are characterised.

items.title: Uniqueness and radial symmetry of magnetic skyrmions
authors: Giovanni Di Fratta, Cyrill B. Muratov, Theresa M. Simon, Valeriy V. Slastikov
items.summary: This paper establishes radial symmetry and uniqueness of magnetic skyrmions as global minimizers of the simplest local micromagnetic energy. The strategy is to show that any radial critical point with strictly decreasing out-of-plane component is the unique minimizer in the class of general degree-one maps with the prescribed limit at infinity. To this end, we identify a class of null Lagrangians that is sufficiently flexible to contain a calibration, giving a uniform lower bound for the energy that is uniquely saturated on the critical point. Our arguments provide a blueprint for proofs of symmetry and uniqueness of minimizers in vectorial variational problems under topological constraints.

items.title: Sound-wave interference reveals the symmetry of a quantum transition
authors: Sergei Studenikin, Yousef Karimi Yonjali, Alex Bogan, Andy Sachrajda, Shabir Barzanjeh
items.summary: A single sound quantum emitted from two places interferes with itself, like a particle passing through two slits. The fringe position reveals whether the sources emit with the same sign (symmetric) or opposite signs (antisymmetric). Knowing this symmetry is important because qubits in solids lose energy by emitting such sound quanta, phonons. For a qubit shared between two sites, antisymmetric emission cancels at long wavelengths, suppressing energy loss, whereas symmetric emission does not. Lifetime measurements give only the total loss and cannot distinguish them. Such fringes appear in double quantum dots, but their position has not been analysed. Here we measure it for single phonons emitted as one hole tunnels between two gallium arsenide quantum dots. Using a quantitative model of sound focusing in the crystal, we find that the two dots emit antisymmetrically, as expected for a moving charge, with only a small symmetric part. Spin-flip transitions in a magnetic field weaken the fringes without shifting them. For double-dot charge qubits, antisymmetric emission is predicted to reduce phonon losses strongly at the frequencies where qubits operate, and phonon interferometry gives a direct way to measure how qubits release energy and to design longer-lived qubits.

items.title: Finite-size scaling and cutoff functions of critical avalanches under cubic saturation
authors: Ryota Kojima, Kazufumi Hosoda, Hiroyuki Suto, Hitoshi Yamada
items.summary: Power-law avalanche statistics characterize the branching bulk but leave open how finite systems terminate their largest events. Here we determine both the finite-size cutoff and the full crossover function connecting the branching regime to the large-event tail for an exchangeable absorbing event process motivated by Cauchy-stable recurrent dynamics. The Cauchy dynamical mean-field theory yields a linear-cubic low-activity drift, while a repeatable-event lift supplies absorbing branching fluctuations. Their competition at criticality generates a distinct finite-size edge controlled by cubic saturation. For avalanches initiated by a fixed microscopic seed, the rescaled edge measure connects the universal branching power law continuously to an exponential large-area tail. This full crossover admits an analytic spectral representation in terms of the boundary spectrum of a quartic Schr\"odinger operator on the half-line: high modes reconstruct the branching singularity, while the ground state fixes the far-tail decay. Exact finite-size calculations and Monte Carlo simulations confirm both the predicted cutoff behavior and the full spectral crossover.

items.title: Dual-Space Analysis of Vortex Configurations and Rotational Energy in a 2D Optical Lattice
items.summary: We investigate the effects of a stationary two-dimensional periodic optical lattice on a rotating Bose--Einstein condensate confined by an isotropic harmonic trap. Within the mean-field description, the condensate is modeled by the two-dimensional Gross--Pitaevskii equation in the rotating frame and solved numerically using an imaginary-time split-step Crank--Nicolson method to obtain stationary vortex states. We examine how the lattice depth, lattice wave vector, particle number, and angular velocity influence the vortex configurations, real-space density, momentum-space density, and energetics of the condensate. We find that the stationary periodic lattice significantly modifies vortex nucleation and spatial organization: vortices emerge progressively with increasing angular velocity and, for sufficiently strong lattice strength, undergo rearrangement and merging. Importantly, changes in the vortex configuration are directly reflected in the momentum-space density, demonstrating that vortex nucleation and rearrangement produce pronounced modifications of the condensate momentum distribution. We further analyze the energy per particle and rotational energy as functions of the angular velocity and find that the presence of the optical lattice substantially alters the rotational response of the condensate. In particular, the rotational energy is progressively reduced at higher angular velocities as the lattice strength is increased. These results demonstrate how a stationary periodic optical lattice modifies vortex formation, momentum-space structure, and rotational energetics of a rotating trapped Bose--Einstein condensate.

items.title: Theory of Berry Singularity Markers: Diagnosing Topological Phase Transitions via Lock-In Tomography
items.summary: This work brings forward an alternative approach for inferring the topological character of phase transitions in insulators. The method relies on subjecting the system of interest to a set of external fields which consist of two parts, i.e., a weak spatiotemporally slowly-varying component on top of a constant offset. This process maps the Berry singularities dictating the bulk band structure of the insulator to a synthetic space spanned by the control parameters of the external fields. By measuring the response of the system to the weak part of the perturbations, when these are additionally chosen to form spacetime textures, one can construct a quantity that is here-termed Berry singularity marker (BSM). The BSM enables the Berry singularity detection as it becomes nonzero only in the close vicinity of a Berry singularity and is equal to its charge. Moreover, near the Berry singularities, the BSM encodes the quantum metric tensor of the system. An advantage of the present method is that it can be implemented in a lock-in fashion, thus allowing to ``filter out'' disorder effects, therefore opening the door to the resilient diagnosis of topological phase transitions.

items.title: Polarons in atomic gases and two-dimensional semiconductors
authors: Pietro Massignan, Richard Schmidt, Grigori E. Astrakharchik, Ata\c{c} \.Imamoglu, Martin Zwierlein, Jan J. Arlt, Georg M. Bruun
items.summary: In this work we provide a comprehensive review of theoretical and experimental studies of the properties of polarons formed by mobile impurities strongly interacting with quantum many-body systems. We present a unified perspective on the universal concepts and theoretical techniques used to characterize polarons in two distinct platforms, ultracold atomic gases and atomically-thin transition metal dichalcogenides, which are linked by many deep parallels. We review polarons in both fermionic and bosonic environments, highlighting their similarities and differences including the intricate interplay between few- and many-body physics. Various kinds of polarons with long-range interactions or in magnetic backgrounds are discussed, and the theoretical and experimental progress towards understanding interactions between polarons is described. We outline how polaron physics, regarded as the low density limit of quantum mixtures, provides fundamental insights regarding the phase diagram of complex condensed matter systems. Furthermore, we describe how polarons may serve as quantum sensors of many-body physics in complex environments. Our work highlights the open problems, identifies new research directions and provides a comprehensive framework for this rapidly evolving research field.

items.title: Direct signatures of Anderson orthogonality catastrophe in nonequilibrium quantum dots
authors: Sarath Sankar, Joshua Folk, Yigal Meir, Eran Sela
items.summary: We propose schemes for unambiguous direct observation of Anderson orthogonality catastrophe (AOC) effects in a quantum dot coupled to a charge detector, enabling experimental estimation of the AOC exponent $\alpha$. We show that certain easy-to-measure observables have a robust dependence on $\alpha$ in the non-equilibrium regimes of source-drain voltage bias or thermal imbalance. Our results are obtained using a rate equation formalism in which the AOC effects on tunnel rates are incorporated in an exact manner, and directly support recent experimental results.

items.title: Unified Learning of Interatomic Potentials and Electronic Hamiltonians, with Applications in 2D Materials
authors: Moon-ki Choi, Daniel Palmer, Shivam Sharma, Harley T. Johnson
items.summary: We introduce UnIPH, an equivariant graph neural network designed to jointly predict both interatomic potentials and tight-binding (TB) Hamiltonians for an atomic structure. UnIPH is trained using density functional theory (DFT) calculations followed by Wannier projection to predict energies and forces as node-level targets and Wannier-projected TB Hamiltonians as edge-level targets. This enables physically consistent modeling of coupled mechanical-electronic responses with near-DFT-level accuracy. After separately training two UnIPH models on DFT data for bilayer graphene and monolayer MoS2, respectively, we find that these models capture key deformation-electronic effects: in twisted bilayer graphene, the trained UnIPH reveals how interlayer spacing, in-plane strain, and out-of-plane corrugation drive isolated flat-band formation, and further shows that modulating substrate interaction strength can generate flat bands even away from the magic angle (approximately 1.1 degrees). For monolayer MoS2, UnIPH accurately reproduces phonon dispersions and strain-dependent band-gap evolution, and further predicts how a non-uniform substrate creates localized strain pockets that spatially modulate the conduction- and valence-band edges.

items.title: Superconductivity of bilayer two-orbital Hubbard model for La$_{3}$Ni$_{2}$O$_{7}$ under high pressure
authors: Wei-Yang Chen, Cui-Qun Chen, Meng Wang, Shou-Shu Gong, Dao-Xin Yao
items.summary: By combining density functional theory (DFT) and density matrix renormalization group calculations, we investigate the unusual pressure dependence of superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$) in the nickelate superconductor La$_{3}$Ni$_{2}$O$_{7}$. Using the hopping integrals and on-site potentials obtained by fitting the DFT band structures, we map a quantum phase diagram of a bilayer two-orbital Hubbard model with increasing pressure in a ladder geometry, which has an intermediate Hubbard repulsion and a Hund's coupling. Near $3/8$ filling, we find a strong spin density wave order, which at $3/8$ filling shows a real-space spin pattern similar to the spin-charge stripe order along a lattice direction. At $21/64$ filling, we find a superconducting phase with interlayer superconductivity (SC) in both the $d_{z^2}$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ orbitals, as well as in-plane SC in the $d_{z^2}$ orbital. Intriguingly, the SC is weakened with increasing pressure and transits to a Luttinger liquid above $80$ GPa, which qualitatively agrees with the experimental observations of decreasing $T_c$ with increasing pressure and a transition to Fermi liquid above $80$ GPa in La$_{3}$Ni$_{2}$O$_{7}$. Through a comparative study, we further show that the ratio of interaction to hopping integral, which reduces moderately with increasing pressure, may play a dominant role in the weakening of SC. Our results of this experimentally relevant model not only find a robust SC through suppressing the competing spin density wave order, but also give new insight into the unusual pressure dependence of SC in La$_{3}$Ni$_{2}$O$_{7}$.

items.title: Multiterminal Quasiballistic Josephson Effect in Monocrystalline Gold
authors: K. B. Polevoy, G. A. Bobkov, D. S. Kalashnikov, A. G. Shishkin, I. V. Trofimov, A. M. Bobkov, E. A. Sedov, E. A. Krivko, M. A. Tarkhov, I. V. Bobkova, V. S. Stolyarov
items.summary: We report on the realization of a planar, quasiballistic Josephson junction array using a Au micron-sized single crystal. The system exhibits a nonlocal, multiterminal Josephson effect, where the supercurrent between any two superconducting leads is governed by the phase coherence across the entire crystal. Key evidence includes a nonmonotonic dependence of the critical current on junction length and magnetic interference patterns with periods corresponding to the shared normal-metal area. Nonlocal transport measurements further confirm that the supercurrent between two electrodes depends on the phase configuration of all the others. Our results, supported by a developed theoretical model, establish a platform for exploring complex superconducting phenomena in multiterminal ballistic systems.

items.title: Theory of planar quasiballistic Josephson junctions
authors: G. A. Bobkov, I. V. Bobkova, A. M. Bobkov, K. B. Polevoy, V. S. Stolyarov
items.summary: We develop a theoretical framework for planar quasiballistic Josephson junctions, where multiple superconducting leads are coupled through a large, nearly ballistic normal metal crystal. Our approach, based on quasiclassical Eilenberger equations, accounts for the dominant role of electron reflections from the crystal surfaces or single impurities, a mechanism distinct from both purely ballistic and diffusive limits. We calculate the critical current between superconducting leads for various geometries, examining its dependence on temperature and magnetic field. Crucially, we demonstrate that in multiterminal setups, the junctions are not independent but form a strongly coupled system. The theory successfully explains key experimental observations from a companion work [Polevoy et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 166001 (2026)], including a non-monotonic dependence of the critical current on the interlayer length, providing a foundation for designing and understanding complex multi-terminal Josephson systems.

items.title: Symmetry-Protected Topological Structures in Quantum Many-Body Scar Subspaces
authors: Chihiro Matsui, Thomas Quella, Naoto Tsuji
items.summary: We investigate how symmetry-associated topological properties, originally defined for ground states, can be consistently extended to dynamically isolated subspaces of quantum many-body systems. Focusing on quantum many-body scars (QMBS), we show that a scar subspace is invariant under the relevant symmetries, and it can support well-defined topological properties inherited from an underlying symmetry-protected topological (SPT) ground state, even though individual scar states need not themselves be symmetric. We refer to such structures as SPT-like scar subspaces, emphasizing that the topological properties are defined at the level of the symmetry-invariant subspace rather than on a state-by-state basis. As a concrete example, we analyze the spin-$1$ Affleck--Kennedy--Lieb--Tasaki (AKLT) model, where a restricted spectrum-generating algebra (rSGA) generates a tower of QMBS on top of a nontrivial SPT ground state admitting a matrix product state (MPS) representation. We demonstrate that the resulting symmetry-invariant scar subspace inherits well-defined topological characteristics, encoded in bond-space symmetry representations, expectation values of symmetry-twist operators, and long-range string order in the dilute regime. We further show that these features persist in a broader class of models, including deformations and higher-spin generalizations that preserve the relevant symmetries and admit nontrivial SPT ground states with MPS representations. Our results provide a general framework in which symmetry-associated topological properties, while inherited from the ground state, are consistently realized at the level of symmetry-invariant nonthermal subspaces. This perspective clarifies how topological structures can be meaningfully defined beyond individual eigenstates.

items.title: Thermomagnonic Torques in Insulating Altermagnets
authors: Edward Schwartz, Hamed Vakili, Alexey A. Kovalev
items.summary: We develop a symmetry-controlled theory of anisotropic thermomagnonic torques in insulating altermagnets. Starting from the stochastic LLG equations, we identify a spin-splitter magnonic torque associated with thermally generated, sublattice-odd spin currents and an anisotropic entropic torque dictated by crystal symmetry. These torques produce anisotropic magnetic-texture responses to temperature gradients. In particular, thermally generated spin currents induce domain-wall precession, which reduces domain-wall velocities for selected gradient directions. We also predict an anisotropic skyrmion Hall response, with symmetry-selected directions enabling fast skyrmion motion with strongly suppressed transverse deflection. Our results reveal experimentally testable symmetry fingerprints of insulating altermagnets and extend more broadly to anisotropic magnets with exchange-driven magnon spin splitting.

items.title: Emergent Elasticity and Quasiconformal Flow in Active Solids
authors: Nikolas H. Claussen, Fridtjof Brauns, Boris I. Shraiman
items.summary: Elasticity theory rests on a constitutive relation between stress and strain relative to a reference state. Living matter, however, generates forces by motor molecule activity independent of strain, requiring a different approach to active tissue mechanics. We develop a theory of two-dimensional continuum mechanics in which the active force configuration, not a reference shape, is the fundamental input. Motivated by the cell-level Active Tension Network model for epithelia, we encode motor-driven intercellular forces in a Riemannian tension metric, whose mapping into physical space relates macroscopic stress to the microscopic tensions. Assuming force balance, we show that a stress-free reference state and an effective stress-strain relation emerge at the tissue scale, making the system an effectively elastic active solid. Extending from statics to dynamics, we show how such a solid can morph its shape through adiabatic evolution of active tensions. To capture plastic cell rearrangement, we introduce a second metric representing the cell adjacency graph in the continuum; topological rearrangement then appears as a continuous reparametrization of the tension manifold. The key fields characterizing the tissue's local mechanical state - tension anisotropy, macroscopic stress, and cell shape - arise from the discrepancies between the tension, adjacency, and physical metrics, represented mathematically by quasiconformal maps. Our theory explains how local contractility controls tissue shape and yields predictions distinct from existing models: tissues can remain rigid while "flowing", with a speed set by the rate of change of active forces rather than their magnitude, and shear flow can occur even under isotropic stress, since macroscopic stress is distinct from local tension anisotropy.

items.title: INTERFACE Force Field for Alumina with Validated Bulk Phases and a pH-Resolved Surface Model Database for Aqueous, Electrolyte, and Molecular Interfaces
authors: Cheng Zhu, Krishan Kanhaiya, Samir Darouich, Sean P. Florez, Karnajit Sen, Patrick Keil, Nawel S. Khelfallah, Eduard Schreiner, Ratan K. Mishra, Hendrik Heinz
items.summary: Alumina and aluminum oxyhydroxides underpin numerous chemical engineering technologies in heterogeneous catalysis, corrosion protection, functional coatings, energy storage devices, and biomedical components. Yet molecular models that predictively connect phase structure, pH dependent surface chemistry, electrolyte organization, and adsorption across operating conditions remain limited. Here we introduce the INTERFACE Force Field (IFF) together with a curated, ready-to-use pH-resolved surface model database for an accurate and transferable atomistic description of major alumina phases according to experimental benchmarks available. The framework covers alpha-Al2O3, gamma-Al2O3, boehmite, diaspore, and gibbsite using a single parameter set compatible with CHARMM, AMBER, OPLS-AA, CVFF, and PCFF. Simulations reproduce experimental reference data across structural, thermodynamic, mechanical, and interfacial benchmarks with deviations of few percent relative to experiment, exceeding existing force fields and density-functional approaches. We introduce a transferable treatment of surface ionization and charge regulation across alumina phases over a broad pH range, enabling simulations of realistic solid-electrolyte interfaces without phase-specific reparameterization. Quantitative reliability is demonstrated by reproducing zeta-potential trends and pH-dependent adsorption of an organic corrosion inhibitor at alumina-water interfaces. Predicted adsorption free energies and surface contact times correlate with experiments across an order of magnitude, enabling process-relevant screening and explaining limitations of earlier adsorption models. The approach is 10,000 to 100,000 times faster than DFT-machine learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) and supports the design of alumina-containing catalysts, corrosion-resistant coatings, energy storage and biomaterials under realistic process conditions.

items.title: Nonreciprocal perfect Coulomb drag in electron-hole bilayers: coherent exciton superflow as a diode
items.summary: Distinguishing an exciton condensate from an excitonic gas or insulator remains a fundamental challenge, as both phases feature bound electron-hole pairs but differ only by the emergence of macroscopic phase coherence. Here, we theoretically propose that a spin-orbit-coupled bilayer system can host a finite-momentum exciton condensate exhibiting a nonreciprocal perfect Coulomb drag -- the coherent-exciton diode effect. This effect arises from the simultaneous breaking of inversion and time-reversal symmetries in the exciton condensate, resulting in direction-dependent critical counterflow currents. The resulting nonreciprocal perfect Coulomb drag provides a clear and unambiguous transport signature of phase-coherent exciton condensation, offering a powerful and experimentally accessible approach to identify, probe, and control exciton superfluidity in solid-state platforms.

items.title: Pathway to lowest-energy structures and stress relaxation for the surface triple junction of copper
authors: Ipen Demirel, Yuan Fang, Yan Liu, Haitian Shan, Xiaopu Zhang, Yuchuan Shao, Jianda Shao, John J. Boland
items.summary: The behavior of surface triple junctions (STJ) at emergent grain boundaries on free surfaces is critical to the microstructure evolution, and therefore to the stability of next generation interconnects. Yet, despite this significant importance, its lowest-energy structure and local stress have remained persistently unknown. Here, we fill this critical gap through high-resolution experimental mapping of the local surface deformation at STJs of a symmetrical tilt grain boundaries with [111] rotation axis and misorientation angles 13.17{\deg}, the analysis of the local core-shifted structure and stress relaxation, and ergodic searching metastable structures accordingly with the molecular-statics (MS) calculation. The computation clearly shows the zipped Y-shaped notch as the lowest-energy structures for this group of STJs, the line profile of which is consistent with the experimental observation. This energetic preference was well explained by the stress delocalization mechanism and was tested for a wide range of boundaries with even deeper core-shift depth using machine learning methods based on the data obtained from MS calculation. By revealing the elusive thermodynamics of STJs, our findings advance the research field by redefining the energetic framework for capillary driven structure evolution and providing foundation for understanding kinetically diffusive deformation and for engineering thin-film interconnects and related materials.

items.title: Rationalizing defect formation energies in metals and semiconductors with semilocal density functionals
authors: Jorge Vega Bazantes, Timo Lebeda, Akilan Ramasamy, Kanun Pokharel, Ruiqi Zhang, John Perdew, Jianwei Sun
items.summary: The study of defects in materials is of utmost importance for technological applications and the design of new materials. In this work, we analyze the performance of density functional approximations on two prototypical sets of defective systems: monovacancies in eight fcc metals, and interstitials in the semiconductor Si-diamond. Specifically, we compute defect formation energies using the local density approximation, the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof generalized gradient approximation, the meta-generalized gradient approximations (meta-GGAs) strongly constrained and appropriately normed (SCAN), its regularized version (r2SCAN), the Lebeda-Aschebrock-Kummel (LAK) meta-GGA, and the Heyd-Scuseria-Ernzerhof screened hybrid functional. For metals, the local density approximation shows better performance compared to the other approximations, whereas for silicon, the meta-generalized gradient approximation Lebeda-Aschebrock-Kummel yields outstand- ing accuracy, surpassing the hybrid functional and approaching the results of more computationally demanding Quantum Monte Carlo methods. To rationalize the different performances, we study the semilocal ingredients rs, s and {\alpha} in both the pristine and defective structures. We identify critical regions that indicate the observed trends of the defect formation energies and pave the way for improving density functional approximations.

items.title: Scar subspaces stabilized by algebraic closure: Beyond equally-spaced spectra and exact solvability
items.summary: We propose algebraic closure as a stabilizing mechanism for quantum many-body scar subspaces, showing that scar states need not rely on an embedded equally spaced spectrum or analytical solvability. We formulate Lie-algebraically closed invariant subspaces and construct local quantum many-body Hamiltonians that preserve an $\mathfrak{su}(N)$-invariant scar subspace but need not act diagonally within it. Such non-diagonal action mixes the conventional tower states while preserving the multidirectional lattice-like spectral structure, allowing nonthermal dynamics and persistent multifrequency oscillations to survive even when individual scar eigenstates become analytically intractable.

items.title: Replica Tensor Train
authors: Miha Srdinsek, Gabriel Gouraud, Xavier Waintal
items.summary: We describe a numerical many-body technique that is based on both tensor networks and quantum Monte Carlo. The variational ansatz is a tensor network that can harvest volume-law entanglement. It is constructed from a tensor train to which one applies a set of non-local operators that force several indices of the tensor train to represent the same physical index, hence its name -- replica tensor train (RTT). From the tensor network toolbox, it inherits the possibility to make linear combinations of these states and apply a certain class of operators. We can therefore find the ground-state of a local Hamiltonian in a purely algebraic way as in standard tensor network algorithms -- i.e. without using gradient descent methods. On the other hand, the volume-law structure forbids calculating physical observables directly. In much the same way as on a quantum computer where one can prepare a state but can only sample it at the end, here we have to use Markov Chain Monte Carlo to compute the observables. We further show that the approach can be extended to build Krylov-subspace ground-state methods within the variational manifold. We illustrate the different algorithms on a two-dimensional spin model with a transverse magnetic field, which can be solved by this approach at low computational cost.

items.title: Bayesian phase transition for the critical Ising model: Enlarged replica symmetry in the epsilon expansion and in 2D
authors: Kay Joerg Wiese, Alapan Das, Adam Nahum
items.summary: A process that images or measures bond energies in the critical Ising model can be in distinct measurement 'phases', depending on the precision of measurement. We study the transition into the strong-measurement phase using replica field theory (an epsilon expansion around six dimensions), a symmetry analysis, and numerical simulations in two dimensions. The results show that certain inference problems possess unexpected structure associated with an enlarged symmetry of the replica description. The symmetry imposes constraints on correlation functions, and is an analog of the Nishimori phenomenon in the Ising spin glass, but in a distinct replica limit. It determines the exact critical exponent for an Edwards-Anderson-like correlator in the measured Ising model, both in 2D and near the upper critical dimension. The symmetry is present microscopically for certain measurement protocols, and it emerges in the infrared for generic protocols at the critical measurement strength. We also examine the epsilon expansion for models with power-law interactions and/or long-range measurement. Finally, we describe an analogous replica symmetry enlargement for measurement in Wegner's lattice gauge theory.

items.title: Constructing Bulk Topological Orders via Layered Gauging
items.summary: Understanding quantum phases and phase transitions in the presence of symmetries is a central objective of quantum many-body physics. A powerful modern paradigm for investigating this problem is topological holography, which relates symmetries in $k$ dimensions to "bulk" topological orders in $(k+1)$ dimensions. While conceptually profound, most existing bulk construction methods rely on sophisticated mathematical formalisms and can be difficult to apply to certain symmetry types. In this work, we propose a physically intuitive and versatile method, termed the layered gauging construction, to systematically generate $(k+1)$-dimensional (liquid or fracton) topological orders from $k$-dimensional generalized symmetries. Roughly speaking, the prescription is to stack many layers of $k$-dimensional quantum systems with certain symmetries into a $(k+1)$-dimensional pile, and then sequentially gauge a diagonal symmetry acting on each nearest-neighbor pair of layers. The detailed procedure depends on the specific symmetry types. We have successfully implemented the method in a number of examples in different spatial dimensions, with symmetries that are conventional, higher-form, subsystem, anomalous, nonabelian, or noninvertible. We hence conjecture the method to be very general. For example, from the subsystem symmetry of the $2d$ plaquette Ising model, we derive the X-cube model and also an anisotropic fracton topological order. Additionally, starting from an anomalous $Z_2$ symmetry in $1d$, we construct a new square lattice model realizing the double semion topological order. From a quantum-error-correction perspective, our layered gauging construction may be viewed as a generalization of the hypergraph-product construction beyond the standard Calderbank-Shor-Steane setting.

items.title: Computing eigenpairs of quantum many-body systems with Polfed.jl
authors: Rok Pintar, Konrad Pawlik, Rafa{\l} \'Swi\k{e}tek, Miroslav Hopjan, Jan \v{S}untajs, Jakub Zakrzewski, Piotr Sierant, Lev Vidmar
items.summary: We present Polfed$.$jl, an open-source Julia package implementing the Polynomially Filtered Exact Diagonalization (POLFED) algorithm for computing mid-spectrum eigenvalues and eigenvectors (shortly, eigenpairs) of quantum many-body Hamiltonians. Access to such eigenpairs is essential for studying non-equilibrium many-body physics, but is hindered by the exponential growth of Hilbert-space dimension. POLFED addresses this challenge through a polynomial spectral transformation evaluated on the fly within a Lanczos iteration, preserving Hamiltonian sparsity and substantially reducing memory costs compared to other diagonalization methods. The package supports flexible energy targeting, automatic optimization of the spectral mapping for structured Hamiltonians, and GPU acceleration, which is particularly effective since the dominant computational cost reduces to repeated sparse matrix-vector multiplications. Benchmarks on disordered spin-chain and fermionic models demonstrate access to larger system sizes than alternative approaches, and CPU--GPU comparisons confirm significant speedups. In particular, we also provide code for constructing the quantum sun model Hamiltonian, a toy model of a many-body ergodicity-breaking transition. While our focus is on many-body Hamiltonians, Polfed$.$jl may be applied to any large sparse matrix.

items.title: First-Principles Study of Fe Adsorption and Its Effects on the Mechanical and Electrical Properties of Monolayer and Bilayer Biphenylene Networks
items.summary: Biphenylene network (BPN), a two-dimensional carbon allotrope, has attracted interest for its potential applications. Here, we systematically investigate Fe adsorption on monolayer and bilayer BPN using first-principles calculations, focusing on structural stability, mechanical properties, and electronic transport. On monolayer BPN, the average Fe adsorption energy generally becomes more negative with increasing Fe coverage, accompanied by nonmonotonic variations and increasingly pronounced Fe aggregation, eventually favoring three-dimensional growth. In bilayer BPN, the interlayer four-membered ring center is the most favorable adsorption site, with a single-Fe adsorption energy of -4.3 eV. Both pristine monolayer and bilayer BPN exhibit high in-plane Young's and shear moduli. Fe adsorption induces nonmonotonic changes in the in-plane stiffness of monolayer BPN, without systematic enhancement. In contrast, interlayer Fe incorporation dramatically enhances the out-of-plane stiffness of bilayer BPN. The effective out-of-plane elastic constant C33 increases from 24.59 GPa in pristine bilayer BPN to 515.63 GPa at an Fe/C ratio of 25%. Furthermore, the transport calculations reveal pronounced in-plane conductivity anisotropy, with substantially different conductivity values normalized by the relaxation time ({\sigma}/{\tau}) along the two crystallographic directions.

items.title: Quantum phase fluctuations quench chiral superconductivity in twisted overdoped cuprate bilayers
authors: Yin Shi, Mengxian Zhao, Fei Yang, Miao Liu, Sheng Meng
items.summary: Twisted cuprate bilayers have been proposed to host chiral superconductivity at temperatures comparable to their large pairing scale, yet experimental signatures of broken time-reversal symmetry remain unclear. We show that quantum phase fluctuations strongly suppress chiral order in twisted overdoped cuprate bilayers despite robust intralayer pairing. At a $45^\circ$ twist, we analytically demonstrate that the chiral transition temperature obeys $T_\chi\propto t^4$ when the single-electron interlayer tunneling amplitude $t$ is weak. This collapse originates from competition between the small Josephson energy scale supporting chirality and the temperature-dependent collective zero-point energy. Chirality consequently survives only in a narrow angular window at ultralow temperatures, with relative-phase plasma softening above the chiral transition. A distinct transport signature arising from the quantum phase fluctuations is a pronounced low-temperature enhancement of the critical current near a magic angle. These findings separate pairing and chiral ordering scales and offer a possible explanation for the difficulty of observing robust chiral superconductivity in twisted cuprates.

items.title: Graph-Based Kirchhoff Modeling of Non-Ohmic Electron Transport in Self-Assembled Nanonecklace Networks
authors: Obed Issakah, Md Khirul Alam Titu, Srivathsan Badrinarayanan, Ravi F. Saraf, Janghoon Ock
items.summary: Gold nanonecklace networks exhibit non-Ohmic current--voltage I-V characteristics with a sharp conduction threshold, making them promising for sensing and transistor-like devices. However, their conduction has been understood largely empirically, because experiments cannot see how conduction evolves inside the network. To address this, we develop a graph-based Kirchhoff modeling framework that resolves these internal processes, tracking the potential and current of every junction. Although every active element conducts linearly, the model reproduces the non-Ohmic response $I \propto (V-V_T)^\zeta$. It also captures the experimentally observed effects of junction properties, network density, and voids, which lends confidence to its predicted internal states. These states show that the non-Ohmic response emerges from voltage-driven percolation. Conduction is governed by how junctions are connected rather than by how many are active, with the current scaling approximately as \(N^{2.3}\) while the number of active junctions grows only linearly. Contrary to the expectation that junction heterogeneity strengthens the nonlinear response, homogeneous junctions in a well-connected network produce the most abrupt and reproducible turn-on. Thus, each structural parameter acts as a distinct control knob. The mean junction characteristics set the threshold, junction uniformity sets the switching sharpness, and network density and voids set the connectivity and current. These relationships provide design rules for tailoring nanonecklace networks to a desired conduction behavior through synthesis and fabrication.

items.title: Dipolar mixtures in checker-board optical bilayers
items.summary: Ultra-cold dipolar mixtures in component-dependent optical potentials constitute an interesting platform for the study of the interplay between intra- and inter-component anisotropic long-range interactions. We study the particular case of binary dipolar mixtures placed in separated bilayers which are displaced in an anti-magic wavelength configuration. Using a combination of second-order perturbation theory and cluster-Gutzwiller calculations, we unveil a rich landscape of possible crystalline phases for the two components, showing that, interestingly, inter-site hopping may result, via super-exchange, in solid-into-solid transitions between different crystalline phases. These crystalline phases and the corresponding transitions can be experimentally realized using e.g. lanthanide mixtures in optical lattices.

items.title: Fluctuation electrodynamics of quantum capacitance in electron bilayers
authors: Dmitry Zverevich, Alberto F. Morpurgo, Alex Levchenko
items.summary: Capacitance provides a thermodynamic probe of interacting electrons. It characterizes the energy cost of transferring charge between conductors, which, in low-dimensional systems, is governed by exchange and correlation effects in addition to electrostatic contributions. We develop a theory of the quantum capacitance of electron double layers, semiconductor quantum wells as well as monolayer and bilayer graphene devices, focusing on the contribution generated by interlayer correlations. Within a functional-integral formulation we show that the separation-dependent part of the ground-state energy is, at the level of ring diagrams, exactly the nonretarded Lifshitz expression for the van der Waals energy of two conducting sheets, with reflection amplitudes built from the layer polarizabilities. The interlayer correction to the inverse capacitance is the second density derivative of this energy: a Casimir compressibility. The zero-point fluctuations that generate Casimir forces between mirrors are here the coupled plasmons of the bilayer, and their contribution to the capacitance is obtained in closed form; its sign shows that interlayer correlations oppose charging at high density. A Gell-Mann-Brueckner analysis gives the high-density limit in terms of universal functions. For graphene we find that monolayers behave like the electron gas, while bilayer graphene is anomalous: interband screening suppresses the correction by orders of magnitude and, within the two-band model, can even reverse its sign in the experimentally relevant range of separations. We delineate the limits of the theory, identifying the dilute Wigner-crystal regime and electron-hole double layers near exciton condensation as regimes where the capacitance becomes a probe of interlayer pairing.

items.title: Bulk-Boundary Correspondence in Semi-Infinite Chains from Sublattice Zeros
authors: Ilya Iakoub, Nicolas Levasseur, Kylian Lionnet, Richard MacKenzie
items.summary: We provide an alternative derivation of the bulk-boundary correspondence for semi-infinite chains. To describe edge states, we analytically continue the usual Bloch Hamiltonian to complex wave vectors k. To start, we note that the zeros of a Bloch wavefunction are related to edge states, at least in systems with nearest-neighbour hoppings. We show that an analytically continued Bloch Hamiltonian with chiral symmetry has exceptional points, where two different states coalesce. These special points are related to the adiabatic protection of edge states. We derive a winding number that counts the exceptional states which, together with the boundary conditions, give a lower bound on the number of edge states protected by chiral symmetry. This bound is saturated in the models we consider.

items.title: Thermal Hall tomography of superconducting topology in rhombohedral graphene
items.summary: Chiral superconductors should carry Majorana modes along their edges, yet three decades of work on candidate materials have not measured the integer that counts them. Rhombohedral graphene offers a new route, because its superconductivity coexists with magnetic domains that can be imaged and rewritten. Here we show how heat transport can read this integer and test it against the domain pattern. Warping and finite pair momentum can close the excitation gap while the band Chern number stays fixed. An exact two-band thermal kernel shows how quantization is then lost and bounds the plateau error when the gap survives. Real-space calculations with disorder show that the integer survives disorder several times larger than the gap, because a mobility gap remains. Bogoliubov pockets instead turn the bulk into a heat conductor, and disorder does not restore quantization. Time-reversed domains should show opposite plateaux, and with ideal contacts a wall between them should carry twice either plateau. In microscopic calculations, a written wall carries this number of Majorana channels even when its core is metallic. Writing, moving and erasing such walls would test superconducting topology, its link to magnetism, and protected heat flow in one device.

items.title: Automated Analysis to Reveal Grain Boundary Phase Microstructures
authors: R. Daniel Moore, Ian S. Winter, Robert E. Rudd, Fadi Abdeljawad, Timofey Frolov
items.summary: We develop a method for analyzing grain boundary (GB) microstructures that identifies distinct interfacial phases and the dislocation line defects separating them. Similar to bulk materials, GBs can adopt multiple distinct interfacial phases and undergo first-order phase transitions. When these phases coexist, their spatial arrangement and phase junctions constitute a GB microstructure, characterized by variations in excess properties and line defects with associated dislocation content. Despite this intrinsic heterogeneity, our ability to quantitatively characterize GB microstructures remains limited, as it requires identification of individual GB phases, phase-resolved excess properties, and the Burgers content of phase junctions, capabilities not available in existing automated methods. Here, we present an automated tool that performs interfacial microstructure mapping for planar coincidence site lattice GBs. The method identifies the spatial distribution of GB phases, quantifies phase-specific excess properties, and estimates the Burgers content of GB phase junctions. We demonstrate the approach using three representative cases: (i) quantification of mass transport during diffusion-limited GB phase transformations; (ii) identification of structurally indistinguishable phases formed by vacancy and interstitial loops; and (iii) characterization of GB microstructures containing phase nuclei. More broadly, this framework enables quantitative studies of GB evolution processes, including spinodal decomposition and coarsening with direct implications for GB deformation, creep, and migration.

items.title: Quantifying Ultrafast Orbital Pumping and Nanometre-Scale Orbital Diffusion in Magnetic Heterostructures
authors: Tongyang Guan, Jiahao Liu, Yuxiao Mo, Liangliang Zhu, Yizheng Wu, Zhensheng Tao
items.summary: Quantifying ultrafast orbital pumping and transport remains challenging because spin and orbital currents contribute coherently to terahertz emission. Here, we combine spintronic terahertz emission spectroscopy with wedge-sample thickness control to disentangle these contributions in Fe, Co and Ni heterostructures with Ta, W and Nb. Their opposite spin Hall and orbital Hall polarities enable quantitative determination of relative pumping strengths and propagation lengths. We find that orbital pumping increases from Fe to Ni, with inferred orbital-to-spin current ratios reaching several tens of percent in Ni, exceeding current microscopic predictions. Remarkably, Nb exhibits an orbital diffusion length of ~1.5 nm, substantially longer than in Ta and W and beyond the sub-nanometre scale predicted by recent orbital-relaxation calculations. These findings provide quantitative experimental benchmarks for ultrafast orbital pumping and transport.

items.title: Irreversibility of many-body harmonic oscillators characterized by generalized Husimi's adiabaticity parameter
items.summary: In a classical paper [K. Husimi, Prog. Theor. Phys. 9, 381 (1953)], Husimi showed that, for a single harmonic oscillator with a time-dependent angular frequency and initial conditions sampled from an equilibrium distribution, the averaged energy cannot decrease after a cyclic operation. This irreversibility is quantified by Husimi's adiabaticity parameter constituted with adiabatic invariants. In this work, we generalize Husimi's framework to a many-body system of one-dimensional harmonic oscillators coupled on an arbitrary connected network, with all spring constants sharing a common time dependence. For a system attached to a fixed wall, the dynamics can be decomposed into independent normal modes by transforming to mass-weighted coordinates and diagonalizing the resulting positive definite matrix, with each mode characterized by its own Husimi's adiabaticity parameter. By defining the generalized Husimi's adiabaticity parameter as their arithmetic mean, we derive the exact time evolution of the averaged energy and establish its non-decrease under cyclic operations. Numerical simulations confirm these results for both a uniform nearest-neighbor chain and a heterogeneous network.

items.title: Quantifying translational and bond-orientational order metrics in hyperuniform and nonhyperuniform many-particle systems
items.summary: Quantifying the degree of order/disorder in many-particle systems remains an outstanding problem in physics, materials science, and mathematics. To this end, we consider the translational order metric $\tau_T$, defined as the squared $L^2$ norm of the total correlation function $h(\mathbf{r})$, and introduce its bond-orientational analogue $\tau_O$, defined from the weighted total correlation function $h_{\mathbf{f}}(\mathbf{r})$ using local orientational weights (S. Torquato et al., Phys. Rev. X 16, 011042 (2026)). The pair $(\tau_T,\tau_O)$ places both forms of order on a common two-point statistical footing. We compute both metrics for two nonhyperuniform sphere-packing models in 2D and 3D as functions of packing fraction $\phi$: 1) equilibrium hard particles and 2) nonequilibrium random sequential addition (RSA) packings. For the nonhyperuniform systems, bond-orientational order remains subdominant along the equilibrium-fluid and RSA configurations; however, its magnitude relative to the translational metric increases near the upper end of the equilibrium-fluid branches, much more strongly in 2D than in 3D, and the two metrics become comparable along the sampled crystal branches. At common packing fractions, equilibrium fluids and RSA packings trace distinct $(\tau_T,\tau_O)$ trajectories, revealing preparation-dependent differences in structural order. As a representative hyperuniform family, we study 2D disordered stealthy hyperuniform (SHU) ground states for $0<\chi<1/2$, where $\chi$ is the stealthiness parameter. Within the disordered SHU phase, bond-orientational order remains subdominant, but its magnitude relative to the translational metric increases toward the disorder-to-order threshold. In all three models, $\tau_T$ and $\tau_O$ are positively correlated beyond the Poisson-reference regime: $\tau_O$ increases monotonically with $\tau_T$ across the sampled state points.

items.title: One-Dimensional Type-IV Collinear Magnetism
authors: Xin Chen, Duo Wang, Peng Zhang, Zeying Zhang
items.summary: Two-dimensional type-IV collinear magnets combine nonrelativistic spin degeneracy with spin-orbit-coupling-enabled magnetic responses. Here we establish a one-dimensional counterpart through altermagnetic confinement. A Lieb-based construction connects three-dimensional altermagnets to two-dimensional type-IV magnets and extends the same principle to one-dimensional ribbons. In a symmetric $[110]$ ribbon, a sublattice-exchange operation preserves the longitudinal momentum and enforces nonrelativistic spin degeneracy. {Spin-orbit coupling (SOC) ties spin to the lattice, so the N\'eel orientation determines whether the remaining symmetries protect the doublets or allow them to split.} First-principles-derived Wannier calculations for Ta$_2$TeSeO ribbons reveal spin-polarized propagating channels with an ideal right-moving-mode polarization of approximately $35\%$ at finite conductance for the parent easy-axis orientation $\mathbf N\parallel[100]$. Direct DFT calculations of Ta$_2$Te$_2$O ribbons resolve the contrast between spin-split $[100]$ and spin-degenerate $[001]$ SOC spectra. Assembling the same isolated Ta$_2$Te$_2$O ribbons into a transversely periodic array restores spin splitting without SOC. This conversion parallels the recovery of three-dimensional altermagnetism through suitable periodic stacking of two-dimensional type-IV magnets. One-dimensional type-IV magnetism thus provides a route to spin splitting through the interplay of antiferromagnetic order and SOC, distinct from conventional Rashba splitting driven by structural inversion asymmetry.

items.title: Spin splitting without symmetry: a nearly compensated ferrimagnet and the origin of altermagnetism
items.summary: The spin splitting of collinear altermagnets is usually attributed to the crystal symmetry relating the opposite-spin sublattices --- a rotation or mirror in place of the translation or inversion of a conventional antiferromagnet. We show that this symmetry organizes the splitting but does not produce it; its origin is the anisotropic arrangement of the magnetic orbitals and their ligands, which also fixes the symmetry itself. Two results establish this. A triclinic ($P1$) \ce{Mn} oxide, a fully compensated ferrimagnet whose two inequivalent sublattices are related by no symmetry, is spin split throughout the Brillouin zone; repositioning the same ligands, atom for atom, to restore an inversion centre relating the two metal sites collapses the splitting to a residual two orders of magnitude smaller, so the splitting follows from the arrangement rather than the symmetry. Symmetry, we show formally, can only ever reverse or forbid a splitting that already exists: it cannot create one between sublattices an arrangement has left electronically identical, nor where the underlying orbitals carry no anisotropy to arrange in the first place. Organizing the analysis through an operation-resolved symmetry hierarchy and reading the crystal classes as a single axis, the enforced nodal planes fall from two to one to zero across the orthorhombic, monoclinic, and triclinic classes while the arrangement-generated splitting persists to the base. The altermagnet and the fully compensated ferrimagnet are thus the two ends of one axis --- the same splitting, organized by symmetry at one end and unorganized at the other --- and the search for compensated spin-split magnets is a search over orbital arrangements rather than symmetry labels.

items.title: Geometry-Driven Suppression of Fermionic Pairing on a Spherical Surface
authors: Lorenzo Frigato, Andrea Tononi, Luca Salasnich
items.summary: We investigate the ground-state properties of a two-component attractive Fermi gas confined to a spherical surface. In the strongly attractive regime, the system forms a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) of tightly bound dimers, yielding a gap and chemical potential that approach flat-space results with leading-order geometric corrections. As the attraction decreases, the system crosses over into a Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) regime, the sphere radius $R$ constrains the Cooper pair size and shell effects emerge. For closed shells, corresponding to magic particle numbers set by the single-particle spectrum, pairing is suppressed above the scattering length $a^*=4R$, whose value is universal in the spherical geometry in contrast with box-trapped fermionic gases. Our results highlight a fundamental interplay among geometry, quantum statistics, and interactions, motivating future experiments with shell-trapped ultracold fermions and inspiring geometry-controlled condensed matter devices.

items.title: Lyapunov-controlled thermalization: an exact real-time example
items.summary: A verified Kubo-Martin-Schwinger (KMS) relation, after a drive has ceased, is not sufficient evidence to prove equilibrium. We demonstrate this in a large-$N$ large-$q$ Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) quench protocol. Although all post-quench fermion correlators are exactly thermal, a second quench back to the initial Hamiltonian reveals hidden memory of the initial state. It is encoded in correlators connecting to times before the first quench. This memory is an extensive nonequilibrium (NEQ) witness with its decay rate being the Lyapunov exponent $\lambda_L$. Thus $\lambda_L$ sets the rate at which the state becomes effectively indistinguishable from a Gibbs state. Despite being a unitary interacting many-body system, the complete NEQ real-time evolution is obtained exactly in the large-$N$, large-$q$ limit, making the setup ideal for analytically studying thermalization.

items.title: A Cross-Entropy Audit (CEA) for Consciousness Tests Moved from Brain to Large Language Model
items.summary: Brain tests of consciousness are often applied to large language models (LLMs). Here consciousness means access: whether information, such as a heard sound, becomes available for report and use. A brain recording is in microvolts and an LLM's internal activations are arbitrary numbers, so the two share no common measurement unit. A brain test of this kind compares competing statistical models of how responses vary over repeated trials. The test's decision names the best-fitting model. The decision is wrong when the test names two states for responses that vary smoothly, or the reverse. No method we reviewed measures how often a transferred test is wrong. We call such a method a transfer audit and propose one, the cross-entropy audit (CEA). First, our audit holds back part of the trials and fits each model to the remaining trials. It then scores how well each fitted model predicts the held-back responses. Comparing two models gives a score difference in nats per trial. That difference does not depend on whether the recording is in microvolts or in activations, so brain and machine are scored on one scale. Second, the audit writes down five choices that such tests make for brain data: the competing models, their fitting, what counts as one independent sample, what the uncertainty interval describes, and the decision rule. Each may need to change on a machine. Third, the audit runs the test on simulated data built to follow one model, so the right decision is known, and counts wrong decisions. In our example, the two models of a two-state test, carried over unchanged to an LLM, found two states in 989 of 12,000 smoothly varying simulated datasets. The audited version of the test found two states in none of them. It detected 599 of 600 two-state datasets. The audited version's uncertainty interval, however, was too narrow at six of the twelve smoothly varying settings and is being repaired.

items.title: Hierarchical Fourier Phase Projection for Local Electronic Observables
authors: Tao Hu, Weiqing Zhou, Zhichang Fu, Yechen Chen, Shengjun Yuan
items.summary: We develop hierarchical Fourier phase projection (HPP) to evaluate electronic observables without explicitly constructing occupied eigenstates. Nested Fourier probes progressively cancel nearby cross terms, while exponential or algebraic density-matrix decay suppresses distant contributions. Refinement reuses all previous matrix-function responses to evaluate diverse electronic observables. Electron density and nonlocal forces illustrate diagonal extraction and off-diagonal contraction, respectively. A locality-based decay model fitted to changes across completed levels estimates residual errors from the unresolved pairs without additional matrix-function applications. Tests using fixed Kohn-Sham Hamiltonians for semiconductors, metals, and thermally perturbed silica cover different decay ranges and periodic cell geometries. About 90% of the assessed density and nonlocal force predictions lie within a factor of two of the reference errors. The probing requirements for a prescribed local accuracy show weak size dependence. This work thus provides a scalable framework linking electronic locality, observable accuracy, and computational effort in large-scale electronic-structure calculations.

items.title: Imaging phase winding in topological superconductors with a fork-tip Josephson STM
items.summary: The topological phase winding in a chiral superconductor remains challenging to access by conventional real-space probes. We propose a scheme to probe this winding with a fork-tip Josephson STM near an impurity, where two superconducting tips form an interferometer sensitive to phase differences between two positions. The phase winding remains accessible via the fork-tip critical current even if the relative phase between the fork-tip and sample fluctuates, establishing a route towards a local phase-sensitive STM probe of topological superconductivity. We numerically compute the interference pattern to demonstrate that the magnitude and phase of the order parameter can be reconstructed as a function of angle, providing a route towards resolving the longstanding open experimental problem of directly detecting phase winding in topological superconductors.

items.title: Time-temperature-composition equivalence of the glass transition in digitally mixed 3D-printed polymers
authors: Beijun Shen, Sanat K. Kumar, Mary C. Boyce
items.summary: For more than seventy years, time-temperature equivalence (TTE) has enabled a few measurements to describe the linear viscoelasticity of polymers over many decades of frequency. Multimaterial 3D printing now combines elastomeric and glassy resins voxel by voxel into digitally mixed polymers. Composition shifts the glass transition along the frequency axis, as temperature does, but also broadens it and increases the rubbery plateau modulus. A translation, the only operation of TTE, cannot capture these changes. Here we establish a time-temperature-composition equivalence (TTCE) from dynamic mechanical measurements of five compositions of a printed family. A shift of the transition along the reduced-frequency axis, a stretch of its breadth and a normalization between its plateaus collapse the storage modulus onto one master curve. The collapse holds at every measured temperature, frequency and composition, through a single reduced variable. The position and breadth of the transition change linearly with the volume fraction of the glassy resin. The phase angle and the relaxation spectrum superpose with the same parameters, so the family shares one distribution of relaxation times. The resulting closed form gives the storage and loss moduli continuously in composition, temperature and frequency, and quantitatively predicts two further mixtures withheld from the calibration. The same shift, stretch and normalization also collapse published temperature sweeps of a patterned composite family of different resins, pointing to broader applicability. Composition thus joins temperature and frequency as a third variable of one equivalence, and the closed form can guide the design of graded and architected printed structures.

items.title: Emergent Spinorial Structure in Mesoscopic Irreversible Thermodynamics
items.summary: Can transport coefficients determine both the coherent evolution of a mesoscopic system and distances between its thermodynamic states? We establish this connection within a canonical operator framework. Thermodynamic coordinates and conjugate forces obey commutation relations governed by a reduced constant ${\kbar}_B$. Requiring coordinate evolution to reproduce self-adjoint flux observables fixes a compatible generator up to an additive multiplication operator, set to zero in the minimal realization. The resulting equation describes coherent mesoscopic amplitudes, with transport fixing its coefficients and the reduced constant setting the evolution scale. An exact first-order factorization gives a geometry through Connes' spectral-distance prescription, including for coordinate-dependent transport. The metric is twice the inverse of the symmetric transport matrix. Coordinate derivatives of the antisymmetric part can change the dynamics without changing distances. Published thermoelectric data illustrate the geometry. A separate quadratic entropy-production observable has adjacent entropy levels separated by the reduced constant under the stated canonical and finite-mode matching assumptions. This conditional prediction offers a possible experimental signature. The evolution is unitary; irreversible relaxation requires additional mechanisms, such as environmental coupling or coarse-graining.

items.title: Transport Determines Spectral Distance in Mesoscopic Thermodynamics
items.summary: We derive a distance between thermodynamic states from a positive Hermitian transport tensor within a mesoscopic canonical model. An exact first-order factorization of the evolution generator gives a commutator norm and the metric $G=2g$, where $g$ denotes the symmetric transport tensor. Gradients of the antisymmetric tensor can change the evolution, but they leave this distance unchanged. The construction allows coordinate-dependent coefficients. For constant Onsager coefficients, a Clifford representation gives the same metric. In a two-channel thermoelectric system, the ratio of normalized principal distances is $\sqrt{1+ZT}+\sqrt{ZT}$. Transport coupling thus fixes the anisotropy of this metric. The construction requires neither an independent metric nor a physical spin variable.

items.title: Moments of Random Permanents and Hafnians: A Replica Approach
authors: Paolo Facchi, Angelo Mariano, Giorgio Parisi, Saverio Pascazio, Antonello Scardicchio
items.summary: Using contour-integral representations of the permanent and of the Hafnian, we turn the computation of their moments for random matrices into a replica calculation, analogous to that of the moments of the partition function of a mean-field spin glass. For the $2k$-th moment of $N\times N$ matrices with independent entries, the dominant saddle point is replica symmetric for $k>2$, and we obtain in closed form the exponential growth rate, the prefactor and the first $1/N$ correction, in agreement with exact enumerations. The growth rate depends only on whether the entries are real or complex; higher cumulants affect only the prefactor and the $1/N$ term. At $k=2$ the replica-symmetric solution becomes unstable, separating a power-law bulk of the distribution from a large-deviation tail, which we compute. The results apply to boson sampling with single photons and with squeezed light.

items.title: Structural characterization of the rutile-GeO2/TiO2 (001) heterointerface
authors: Imteaz Rahaman, Martha R. McCartney, David J. Smith, Kai Fu
items.summary: Rutile-GeO2 (r-GeO2) has emerged as a promising ultrawide-bandgap (UWBG) semiconductor for future high-power device applications because of its favorable combination of physical and electrical properties. This study has used high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM) to compare heterointerfaces between thin films of GeO2 grown by metal-organic chemical vapor deposition on closely-lattice-matched rutile TiO2 (r-TiO2) substrates at temperatures of 840{\deg} C and 925{\deg} C. Cross-sectional TEM observations reveal interfaces with two entirely different structures: an amorphous GeOx/r-TiO2 heterostructure with an abrupt, highly faceted and non-planar interface, or a fully epitaxial r-GeO2/r-TiO2 heterostructure characterized by a more wavy but often facetted interface. Structural analysis of the latter sample revealed a high density of strain-relieving interfacial dislocations, identified primarily as Lomer-type or 60{\deg}-type, that accommodated the ~4% lattice mismatch between the two materials, while chemical analysis showed very limited interfacial intermixing. Crystallographic analysis showed that the interface faceting was associated with rutile {101} facets, with characteristic facet angles of ~114{\deg}; these observations support thermally driven TiO2 (001) substrate faceting rather than an interface reconstruction resulting from GeO2 epitaxy. Overall, these findings provide useful insights into the mechanisms governing interface formation and strain relaxation in r-GeO2/r-TiO2 heterostructures and suggest that further refinement of growth conditions should enable improved epitaxial growth of r-GeO2 for future ultrawide-bandgap electronic device applications.

items.title: A Self-Consistent Two-Carrier Drift-Diffusion Framework for p-n Junctions: Extended Diode Equation, Power Dissipation, and Base Transit Time
authors: Jianhong Yang, Tinglan Li, Gonghao Sun
items.summary: The classical theory of p-n junctions derives the current-voltage characteristic from minority-carrier diffusion alone: majority carriers are treated as an inert background, the quasi-neutral base as field-free, and the junction voltage as equal to the applied bias. These premises fail together under high bias and high-level injection, where the observed current roll-off is reproduced only by appending an empirical series resistance outside the junction physics. Here we develop a self-consistent two-carrier drift-diffusion framework that introduces no assumption beyond the classical ones. Excess majority carriers are shown to be electrostatically forced transport participants: the ambipolar diffusion equation, closed by exact two-sided boundary conditions, yields a unified excess-carrier profile. The resulting base field separates into an ohmic and a Dember component, and all four current components follow in closed form, their sum being position independent. At device level the framework closes into an extended diode equation that contains the Shockley equation as its low-injection, long-base limit and reproduces the n=2 roll-off intrinsically. The junction voltage emerges as a self-limiting drop confined to the space-charge region and separated from the applied bias by exact base drops. Two device-level corrections are quantified: at high current, 75-90% of the dissipation migrates from the junction into the quasi-neutral base, and field-assisted acceleration shortens the base transit time by up to a factor of six. Three parameter-free predictions follow: a universal ideality-factor crossover that passes through 3/2 when the boundary excess equals the doping, a high-injection onset voltage that scales as 119 mV per decade of doping, and a geometry factor that survives into high injection.

items.title: Momentum-selective graphene spectroscopy of moir\'e excitons
items.summary: Far-field photoluminescence probes only the light-cone corner of an exciton's momentum content, whereas energy transfer to nearby graphene integrates in-plane momenta up to the inverse spacer thickness $1/z$. For a WSe$_2$/MoSe$_2$ heterobilayer we build the transition polarization $\bm{P}_n(\qv)$ of each localized moir\'e exciton from the registry-dependent vector dipole texture and use each $\bm{P}_n$ for both baths. The two baths rank the states differently: the graphene-rate ratios differ from the optical ones, their ordering inverts with spacer thickness, and the distance exponents at $z=10$\,nm spread by more than two units. These ratios are independent of the transition-dipole prefactor. Within the $C_3$-symmetric leading-harmonic model the chiral $p_+$ and $d_-$ states are also dark at normal incidence yet transfer to graphene at rates comparable to the bright ground state. Their graphene rate depends on the sign of the texture phase, a quantity invisible in far-field emission, which we determine from first principles. In a device this prediction requires a splitting, larger than the symmetry-breaking mixing, that protects the chiral partners. Graphene proximity thus acts as a momentum-selective near-field probe of moir\'e excitons, and we propose its use as a practical spectroscopy.

items.title: Simplified Parisi Ansatz III: Constructive Cavity Method and Ultrametricity
items.summary: We present a physical explaination of the Constructive Cavity Method (CCM) for the Sherrington--Kirkpatrick model, which identifies the decomposition of the cavity variables into layers with the random overlap structure of Aizenman--Sims--Starr. We describe the low-temperature excitations through a dilute gas of defects relative to the ground state. The sharing of these defects among the descendants and the renewal of the fluctuations along new branches produce the GREM structure and the ultrametricity of the overlaps. This mechanism is developed first with a finite number of defects and then extended to exponential populations of states. At fixed kernel, the Gaussian covariances of the fresh fields connect the complete cavity variables, including their common components, to the same hierarchy that determines the Gibbs masses. We also correct some ambiguities of earlier formulations.

items.title: Large superconducting diode effect indicates nonuniform triplet pairing in UTe2
authors: Zheyu Wu, Daniel Shaffer, Dmitry V. Chichinadze, Mengmeng Long, Hanyi Chen, Andrej Cabala, Theodore I. Weinberger, Maurice Bal, Steffen Wiedmann, Dave Graf, Vladimir Sechovsk\'y, Michal Vali\v{s}ka, F. Malte Grosche, Alex Levchenko, Alexander G. Eaton
items.summary: The superconducting diode effect (SDE) is characterized by unequal critical current magnitudes for opposite-polarity current flow, owing to broken spatial-inversion and time-reversal symmetries. For a superconducting pair wavefunction to spontaneously break inversion symmetry implies the formation of Cooper pairs with nonzero momentum, yielding a nonuniform superconducting state. For singlet superconductors, the formation of such a (FFLO) state has long been understood to provide an escape from high field Pauli pair-breaking -- how and why such an effect might occur for equal spin pairing is an open question. Here we report the observation of a large SDE in bulk specimens of the three-dimensional heavy-fermion triplet superconductor UTe$_2$, with a peak diode efficiency of 33% at the high magnetic field strength of 33.6 T, representing the highest-field observation of the SDE to date. Crucially, this nonreciprocal transport is strictly confined to a narrow field regime where superconductivity coexists with a field-induced spin-polarized state near a first-order metamagnetic phase boundary. The absence of the SDE away from this slender phase-intersection argues strongly against purely extrinsic vortex pinning asymmetries. Instead, our findings indicate spontaneous inversion symmetry breaking accompanied by finite-momentum Cooper pairing. We model this behavior using a phenomenological Ginzburg-Landau theory, demonstrating that the intertwining of magnetic and triplet superconducting orders can stabilize an odd-parity FFLO state.

items.title: Nano-Nb Superconducting 3D Josephson Junctions Arrays in Cu-Normal Matrix: Superconducting Phase Coherence and Quantum Fluctuations Properties
authors: R. L. de Almeida, J. Albino Aguiar, C. A. C. Passos, S. K. Sharma, J. A. H. Coaquira
items.summary: We investigate the superconducting behavior, phase coherence, and quantum fluctuation properties of three-dimensional arrays of nanometric Nb Josephson junctions embedded in a normal Cu matrix ($\text{Cu-}x\text{ wt}\%\text{Nb}$, $x = 3, 5, 15,$ and $20$), with emphasis on the $5$ and $15$ compositions. Magnetic properties were measured by dc magnetization as a function of temperature and magnetic field using a SQUID magnetometer and by ac susceptibility. Transport properties, including magnetoresistance, $V(I)$ curves, and the critical current $I_c(H,T)$, were measured at fields up to $90\text{ kOe}$. A micro-Hall sensor with ten transverse voltage bridges ($5.0 \times 0.2 \times 0.01\text{ }\mu\text{m}^3$) was used to calibrate the magnetic field actually applied to the sample. Magnetization and transport measurements reveal a double superconducting transition that depends on the applied field and current: $T_c(H)$, with $T_c(0) = 8.2\text{ K}$, is associated with the intragranular response of the Nb grains, whereas the lower $T_c(H)$ is associated with Josephson coupling between grains through the Cu matrix. The response combines that of bulk Nb with signatures of weakly coupled grains, consistent with a collection of superconducting grains embedded in a nonsuperconducting matrix. The characteristic fields $H_{c1} = 400.03\text{ Oe}$ and $H_{c2} = 15\text{ kOe}$ (grains), and $H_{c1j} = 99.93\text{ Oe}$ and $H_{c2j} = 199.25\text{ Oe}$ (intergranular coupling), were determined. The critical current $I_c(H,T)$ exhibits a central maximum at low fields, followed by a long tail and small oscillations with a period of $\Delta H \approx 24\text{ Oe}$, attributed to quantum interference between coupled grains. At higher fields, magnetic flux gradients destroy phase coherence and randomize the phase $\theta$ of the order parameter $\psi = |\psi|e^{i\theta}$, suppressing the oscillations.

items.title: The Flexoelectric Twist: Persistence of Heavy Fermion Picture in Small-Angle Twisted Bilayer Graphene
authors: Qirong Yao, Ka Cheuk Fan, Tianyu Qiao, Hao Shi, Jiangchang Zheng, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Xi Dai, Berthold J\"ack
items.summary: Twisted bilayer graphene (TBG) near the first magic angle ($\theta\approx1.05^{\circ}$) hosts topological flat bands that provide a fertile ground for exploring strongly correlated phases. At smaller twist angles ($\theta<1^{\circ}$), lattice relaxation profoundly alters the moir\'e landscape. The extent to which moir\'e lattice reconstruction at different length scales affects the electronic structure through electro-mechanical coupling remains unresolved. Using scanning tunneling microscopy on small-angle TBG devices with different twist angles $\theta\approx0.3-0.7^{\circ}$, we observe a pronounced $dI/dV$ peak at the AA site of the moir\'e lattice on top of a spectrum that is asymmetric about the charge neutrality point; we visualize lattice reconstruction at moir\'e lattice length scales (20-45\,nm); and we detect a dilation of the atomic lattice at the AA sites at Angstrom length scale. We demonstrate that the inclusion of moir\'e lattice reconstruction supports compact localized heavy fermion $f-$states at AA sites whereas the inclusion of atomic lattice dilation generates a strong flexo-electric response that breaks particle-hole symmetry, pushing the $f$-states down in energy. Consequently, these heavy fermion states energetically coexist with itinerant $c$-electrons at the AB/BA sites. Our spatially resolved spectroscopic measurements visualize this coexistence, confirming the persistence of the heavy fermion model in the small-angle regime $\theta<1^{\circ}$. Our findings show that flexo-electric responses can realize qualitatively distinct electronic landscapes in moir\'e materials beyond the single-particle picture. Looking ahead, small-angle TBG could prove an ideal platform to explore the interacting large-$N$ Kondo lattice problem with high tunability of the $f-$occupation and $c-$density through twist-angle and electrostatic back gates, respectively.

items.title: New horizons for inhomogeneous quenches and Floquet CFT
items.summary: -cross Abstract: A fruitful avenue in investigating out-of-equilibrium quantum many-body systems is to abruptly change their Hamiltonian and study the subsequent evolution of their quantum state. If this is done once, the setup is called a quench, while if it is done periodically, it is called Floquet driving. We consider the solvable setup of a two-dimensional CFT driven by Hamiltonians built out of conformal symmetry generators: in this case, the quantum dynamics can be understood using two-dimensional geometry. We investigate how the dynamics is reflected in the holographic dual three-dimensional spacetime and find new horizons. We argue that bulk operators behind the new horizons are reconstructable by virtue of modular flow.

items.title: The entanglement membrane in 2d CFT: reflected entropy, RG flow, and information velocity
authors: Hanzhi Jiang, M\'ark Mezei, Julio Virrueta
items.summary: -cross Abstract: The time evolution of entanglement entropy in generic chaotic many-body systems has an effective description in terms of a minimal membrane, characterised by a tension function. For 2d CFTs, a degenerate tension function reproduces several results regarding the dynamics of the entropy; this stands in contrast to higher dimensions where the tension is non-degenerate. In this paper we use holography to show that, in order to correctly capture the reflected entropy in 2d CFT, one needs to add an additional degree of freedom to the membrane description.
